title: Ezekiel 13:17–23
context: The LORD tells Ezekiel to set his face against women who prophesy out of their own heart and use magic bands and veils to hunt souls, for handfuls of barley and pieces of bread. The exact nature of these practices is uncertain; they seem to involve divination or magic used to manipulate people, and the imagery is best read soberly. The LORD promises to tear away the bands and veils and set his people free, because the women’s lies have discouraged the righteous and strengthened the wicked so that they did not turn and live. Both traditions read the passage as shared ground about God’s care for people misled by false spiritual guidance.

verses.text: You, son of man, set your face against the daughters of your people, who prophesy out of their own heart; and prophesy against them,
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD tells Ezekiel to set his face against the daughters of his people who prophesy out of their own heart. Women who claim to prophesy are now addressed.

Arminian readers see the same standard applied to all who speak falsely in God’s name.
verses.reformedNotes:
The charge mirrors 13:2; the concern is false prophecy, not that women prophesy (compare Huldah, 2 Kings 22:14).

Reformed readers see God judging false claims impartially. Both traditions read this as shared ground.

verses.text: and say, “The Lord GOD says: ‘Woe to the women who sew magic bands on all elbows and make veils for the head of persons of every stature to hunt souls! Will you hunt the souls of my people and save souls alive for yourselves?
verses.arminianNotes:
The Lord GOD pronounces woe on the women who sew magic bands and make veils “to hunt souls.” Their practices ensnare people.

Arminian readers see people led astray by manipulation.
verses.reformedNotes:
The exact nature of the bands and veils is uncertain; proposals include amulets or objects used in divination or magic. The imagery is best read soberly.

Reformed readers see God opposing those who exploit others. Both traditions read this as shared ground.

verses.text: You have profaned me among my people for handfuls of barley and for pieces of bread, to kill the souls who should not die and to save the souls alive who should not live, by your lying to my people who listen to lies.’
verses.arminianNotes:
They have profaned God among his people for handfuls of barley and pieces of bread, killing souls who should not die and keeping alive those who should not live. Their lies have deadly effects.

Arminian readers see profit corrupting spiritual counsel.
verses.reformedNotes:
The verse may describe false promises and threats that misled people about life and death, though the details are uncertain.

Reformed readers see God’s honor profaned. Both traditions read this as shared ground and hedge the specifics.

verses.text: “Therefore the Lord GOD says: ‘Behold, I am against your magic bands, with which you hunt the souls to make them fly, and I will tear them from your arms. I will let the souls fly free, even the souls whom you ensnare like birds.
verses.arminianNotes:
The Lord GOD is against their magic bands, with which they hunt souls like birds, and will tear them from their arms and let the souls go free. God will free the ensnared.

Arminian readers see God rescuing those caught by deception.
verses.reformedNotes:
The bird-trapping imagery pictures entrapment and release.

Reformed readers see God’s power to deliver his people. Both traditions read this as shared ground about God breaking the hold of falsehood on those who were deceived.

verses.text: I will also tear your veils and deliver my people out of your hand; and they will no longer be in your hand to be ensnared. Then you will know that I am the LORD.
verses.arminianNotes:
God will tear their veils and deliver his people from their hand, so they will no longer be ensnared. Deliverance is promised.

Arminian readers see God acting to free his people from manipulation.
verses.reformedNotes:
The verse stresses God’s protection of “my people” from those who exploited them.

Reformed readers see God’s faithfulness in delivering his own. Both traditions read this as shared ground about God’s care for those harmed by false spiritual leaders and his intention to set them free.

verses.text: Because with lies you have grieved the heart of the righteous, whom I have not made sad; and strengthened the hands of the wicked, that he should not return from his wicked way, and be saved alive.
verses.arminianNotes:
With lies they have grieved the righteous, whom God had not made sad, and strengthened the wicked so that he would not return from his wicked way and be saved alive. Lies discourage repentance.

Arminian readers see deception hindering a real turning.
verses.reformedNotes:
The concern for the wicked to return and live is developed in 18:23.

Reformed readers see falsehood confirming people in sin. Both traditions read this as shared ground.

verses.text: Therefore you shall no more see false visions nor practice divination. I will deliver my people out of your hand. Then you will know that I am the LORD.’ ”
verses.arminianNotes:
They will no longer see false visions or practice divination; God will deliver his people from their hand. The section ends with deliverance.

Arminian readers see God ending a practice that harmed his people and opening the way back to truth.
verses.reformedNotes:
The closing refrain again ties God’s action to the knowledge of the LORD.

Reformed readers see God protecting his people from deception. Both traditions read this as shared ground about God’s commitment to truth and to the welfare of those misled.
